Simmons, shown last year with fourth, is one of the top names for Il Lombardia. (Photo: Sara Cavallini/Getty Images)

The leaves are falling, the season is fading, and cycling’s final monument is wide open at this weekend’s Il Lombardia .

Brandon McNulty , Remco Evenepoel, Paul Seixas , and Isaac del Toro headline the contenders for Il Lombardia on October 10.

With five-time defending champion Tadej Pogačar sidelined with injury, the elite men’s road season’s final big date will see a peloton keen to fill the void.

For the first time since 2020, somebody with the last name other than Pogačar will lift the trophy.

Will that make it a better race? We’re about to find out.

The Slovenian’s absence could give Evenepoel a chance to win his first Lombardia victory. He’ll square off with recently crowned world champion McNulty and a deep field of favorites.

Nobody gets an easy ride going into the offseason. Il Lombardia is the last real hit-out in what’s been a wild and thrilling 2026 road season.

The 120th edition packs 239km and 4,600m of climbing between Bergamo and Como, with the Ghisallo, Civiglio, and two trips up San Fermo della Battaglia waiting to squeeze out whatever juice the legs might have left.

Here’s everything you need to know about the 2026 “Race of the Falling Leaves,” aka Il Lombardia.

Date : Saturday, October 10 Edition : 120th Start : Bergamo, Italy Finish : Como, Italy Distance : 239km Elevation gain : 4,600m Climbs : Nine, counting the early Bocche di Gavarno rise Start : 10:45 a.m. CET Expected finish : 4:40 to 5:20 p.m. CET Defending champion : Tadej Pogačar, sidelined with injury Nickname : Race of the Falling Leaves

Il Lombardia switches direction for 2026, starting in Bergamo and finishing in Como after the reverse route in 2025.

That matters because the Como finish brings the steep Civiglio climb and its twisting descent into the late-race equation, followed by one final haul over San Fermo della Battaglia.

The opening climbs around Bergamo give the breakaway room to move and the peloton plenty of opportunity to settle in for a long day.

The route then crosses Brianza, drops toward Lecco, and follows Lake Como to Bellagio for the ascent of the Madonna del Ghisallo.

From there, the race heads toward Como and a finale built around San Fermo, Civiglio, and San Fermo again.

The course rolls out from Bergamo and opens with Bocche di Gavarno, Selvino, Colle di Berbenno, and Valpiana before reaching the sharper climbs toward Como. The early breaks will move and the chase is on.

Giovenzana adds a new challenge with about 100km remaining. The 3.6km ascent averages 9.2 percent, with a 750-meter section at 14 percent and ramps reaching 16 percent.

The iconic Madonna del Ghisallo hits out above Bellagio, climbing 8.6km at 6.2 percent to the iconic sanctuary overlooking Lake Como.

The final circuit packs Civiglio between two ascents of San Fermo della Battaglia. Civiglio climbs 4.2km at 9.7 percent, with a narrow road and a twisting descent that sprung Vincenzo Nibali to victory in 2015 and 2017.

San Fermo bites at 2.7km at 7.2 percent. Its second ascent is the final climb, topping out at about 5km from the finish before a fast descent into Como and a flat final kilometer.

Action guaranteed until the end. The tifosi will be out in droves.

Just like when he’s in a race, Pogačar’s absence also changes the entire conversation.

A Pog-free Lombardia is one without the overwhelming defending favorite to dictate how everybody else races.

Several teams start with more than one potential winner in what should be a wide-open race.

Evenepoel, McNulty, and an on-form and angry Ciccone top the list, with Seixas, Del Toro, Juan Ayuso, Matteo Jorgenson, Quinn Simmons , and Tom Pidcock among the other top names on the provisional start list.

Remco Evenepoel: His best Lombardia chance yet

Evenepoel arrives coming off his spectacular European championship bike-throw, and he’s been runner-up in the past two editions of Lombardia.

He already owns two Liège-Bastogne-Liège titles, so winning Saturday would give him a third monument victory and his first at Lombardia.

Without Pogačar, the Belgian becomes the five-star favorite. Rivals won’t want to give him any daylight, especially anywhere on the final circuit.

Brandon McNulty : Rainbow jersey, monument dreams

McNulty brings the world champion’s jersey into a race no American has won.

His Montréal victory confirmed his potential on long, attritional races. A strong week in his rainbow jersey debut bodes well for a big ride this weekend.

UAE also brings del Toro, giving the superteam another attacking option as it tries to keep the trophy in-house.

Giulio Ciccone and Juan Ayuso : Two cards for Lidl-Trek

Ciccone heads to Lombardia after his agonizing photo finish defeat to Evenepoel at the European championships.

The steep Como finale suits his climbing strengths, and racing on home roads adds another incentive to try to become Italy’s first winner since Nibali’s second in 2017.

Alongside Ayuso, Lidl-Trek packs two riders capable of playing the odds.

Simmons — who rode a monster race last year to finish fourth — is also confirmed for Lidl-Trek.

Seixas and del Toro won’t be content to follow the wheels.

Both have the climbing legs to go deep into the race, and both are chasing redemption after the Montréal worlds.

The tactical question is whether they will hide in the bunch until the final climbs or force the selection themselves early.

For either one to win, they’ll have to get past each other. Neither has won a monument yet. This could be their best chance.

Matteo Jorgenson, Tom Pidcock : The other contenders

Jorgenson and Pidcock both showed top form at Tre Valli, even if Jarno Widar outplayed them in the final sprint.

Davide Piganzoli, Giulio Pellizzari, and Antonio Tiberi add to the Italian options. Ben Healy is always a name to watch in any climb-heavy race.…

Remco Evenepoel, shown here with world champion Brandon McNulty, spoke out on behalf of the peloton over rider safety. (Photo: Dario Belingheri/Getty Images)

The riders have had enough, and the bunch delayed Il Lombardia for five minutes Saturday morning to demand safer roads after another ugly week of vehicles getting onto race courses .

World champion Brandon McNulty and European champion Remco Evenepoel stood at the front as the peloton held up the season’s final monument to demand rider safety .

Evenepoel grabbed the microphone and spoke for the riders in a rare public showing of solidarity.

“In the name of the whole bunch and not only for the guys that are here but for everybody pro cycling, we want to make this statement because there’s too many incidents happening with vehicles in the race,” Evenepoel said.

“Unfortunately, we lost the life of a brother and of a colleague of us,” he said. “We want to make this statement to just show to the whole world that we cannot keep accepting the fact that guys are getting injured and are literally dying while doing what we like the most.”

The riders and the CPA also issued a joint statement asking the UCI and race organizers to take responsibility and tighten course security ( see statement below ).

Frustration has been bubbling behind the scenes ever since 19-year-old Finlay Tarling was killed following a collision with a vehicle that entered the Volta a Portugal course in August.

Michael Tarling, the father of Finlay, took to X to support the solidarity among the riders.

“We are so thankful, moved and proud of Fin’s fellow cyclists today for making a stand at the Tour of Lombardy,” he wrote. “Things need to change and no other family should ever receive the phone call we received on 14th Aug. We sincerely hope the UCI are listening and changes will be made.”

‼️ La protesta del pelotón, encabezada por Remco Evenepoel, antes del inicio de #IlLombardia ⚠️ El movimiento llega tras los últimos incidentes con vehículos de carrera estas semanas #LaCasadelCiclismo pic.twitter.com/OgEwYGlIwq

Saturday’s protest comes on the heels of high-profile vehicle incidents at both Coppa Bernocchi and Tre Valli Varesine this week in Italy.

At Monday’s Coppa Bernocchi, a DHL delivery van pulled onto the route from a side street and drove behind the breakaway before stopping.

A day later, a police motorbike traveling against the direction of racing collided with Tom Pidcock’s Pinarello-Q36.5 teammates Thomas Gloag and Marcel Camprubí at Tre Valli Varesine.

Gloag abandoned and required stitches to his knee , while Camprubí continued and later complained that “nothing changes.”

Heavy crashes have marked racing this week in Italy as well .

The latest incidents add to a grim toll the past few years. Gino Mäder died after crashing at the 2023 Tour de Suisse, André Drege died while descending at the Tour of Austria in 2024, and junior racer Muriel Furrer died following a crash at the 2024 UCI Road World Championships.

“This is why we want to stand for five minutes more, to make our statement towards organizations, to the public, to everybody that is following cycling and accepting the fact that people are dying,” Evenepoel said.

The UCI has introduced new safety measures , including better barriers and signage, but riders want faster action and stronger protection on race roads.

“We want to pay our tribute and respect to everybody that was already involved in the incidents,” he said.

After the protest, the race started without further incident.

There was no immediate response from the UCI.

As riders, we stand united against the unnecessary risk our lives are being subjected to.

This week alone, there were multiple incidents of vehicles on race courses. Two riders crashed when they hit a motorbike who was driving the wrong way on the race route. Luckily both escaped with cuts and bruises, it could have been so much worse.

This summer, a life was tragically lost to exactly this kind of failure. We will not stand for this any longer.

Riders race at high speed with little protection, and we depend on the race organisers to secure the roads. That responsibility is not being met.

We are calling for the help of the UCI for race organisers to take accountability and act. That means a serious, open conversation between riders, race organisers and the UCI resulting in concrete changes to how race routes are secured and managed.

After five minutes, we raced as normal. We did not want to affect the race, only to show what riders can do when we stand as one.

We love this sport. We respect the race organisers. We want to race hard and put on a show for our fans. However most importantly we want to come home safe to our loved ones.

Magnus Sheffield, shown here at the 2025 Paris-Nice, joins Uno-X on a four-year deal. (Photo: DAVID PINTENS/BELGA MAG/AFP via Getty Images))

Magnus Sheffield is heading to Uno-X Mobility in a blockbuster move that brings the American all-rounder a little closer to home.

New York raised, yes. But Sheffield’s Norwegian roots run much deeper than his first name.

“Joining Uno-X Mobility feels like closing the circle on the journey my mum started when she moved to the US at 20. Uno-X has always been a team I was interested in, even before I became a professional,” Sheffield said in Wednesday’s announcement. “It was never a question of if, only when.”

The 24-year-old holds both American and Norwegian passports, grew up speaking Norwegian at home, and has family scattered around Oslo.

Now he’ll be racing with Uno-X through 2030.

Sheffield will be the first American to race on the team and first rider who isn’t Norwegian or Danish since its pro-level arrival in 2020.

Sheffield will leave Netcompany-Ineos after five seasons, having stepped up from Rally Cycling in 2022.

A New Yorker by birth, he won Brabantse Pijl at 19 during his first spring with the British team.

A Paris-Nice stage victory in 2025 and sixth at the 2024 Tour of Flanders are other hints of why Uno-X signed him to a multi-year deal.

General manager Thor Hushovd thinks there’s plenty left in the tank.

“Magnus is a rider with enormous potential, and I don’t think we have seen the full extent of it yet,” Hushovd said. “He has already finished fourth in Paris-Nice and sixth in Flanders. That tells you a lot about the range he has.”

For Uno-X, which stepped into the WorldTour in 2026, Sheffield’s four-year deal is the next big move of his career.

“This is one of the big signings for us, and one we are very proud of,” Hushovd said. “We believe we can give him the environment to take another step and develop into one of the leading riders in the sport.”

Sheffield joins an incoming group that includes Casper Pedersen (Soudal Quick-Step), Felix Ørn-Kristoff (Lotto Intermarché), and Kristian Egholm from (Lidl-Trek Future Racing) — all Danes and Norwegians, of course.

Maybe call him half-Norwegian. His deep family ties to Norway help explain why both sides see this as such a good fit.

“Language is an important part of the identity we have built as a team. Magnus understands the culture and can become part of it naturally from day one,” Hushovd said. “And on top of everything he can do on the bike, he is an incredibly good guy.”

And speaking Norwegian in team meetings?

That won’t be a problem. He already speaks it fluently.

“My mum grew up in Gjøvik, and most of our family now lives around Oslo. She moved to the U.S. to study when she was 20, and that’s where she met my dad,” he said. “We always spoke Norwegian at home. It was almost our secret family language growing up in the U.S.”

Family visits and Norwegian traditions were part of Sheffield’s childhood long before cycling became his day job.

His sister now lives in Norway, and his brother spent several years there before returning to the United States to study.

Now he’s bringing that connection into the WorldTour.

Ben Oliver gave Modern Adventure its biggest wins in 2026. (Photo: Pim Waslander/Soccrates/Getty Images)

Modern Adventure Pro Cycling winds down its debut season in Europe this weekend, with five wins on the board and a season packed with highs and lows.

The first new U.S. men’s team with major European ambitions in more than a decade raced Binche-Chimay-Binche on Tuesday before signing off Sunday at Paris-Tours .

Not a bad first lap around the calendar.

Harry Lasker rode into the early break Tuesday in Belgium, while Ben Oliver leads the team’s hopes for the French season finale.

Since lining up in February, Modern Adventure has been in the frame all season long .

The squad comes into its final races after a strong week at the Tour de Langkawi, where Riley Pickrell delivered a stage win and three second places.

Pickrell finally got the better of Matteo Malucelli on stage 6 for the Canadian’s third pro win and his first for Modern Adventure.

“When you finally do get a win, it really feels like you’re paying your teammates back,” he said. “I can’t be happier.”

Lead-out man Scott McGill collected a yellow card in what’s all part of racing for the first-year squad.

Commissaires cited McGill under the rule for decelerating during a sprint and endangering others.

Pickrell added another second place in Sunday’s finale, while Stefan de Bod finished 16th overall.

Not bad for the team’s final stage race of 2026 .

Simply getting the team onto the start line this season counted as an early win for George Hincapie ’s project.

With the help of key backers, Hincapie signed the riders, built the staff and infrastructure , and put rubber to the road in the team’s pro debut at the AlUla Tour in February.

“I wanna look back in five, six years from now and go, this is where we started,” Hincapie told Velo earlier this season. “From basically ‘Bad News Bears’ to building to be one of the best teams in the world.”

Hincapie launched Modern Adventure with ambitions to reach the Tour de France within the next five years and give U.S. talent a foothold in the European peloton.

Race organizers gave the new kids a chance after Hincapie dug into his Rolodex of contacts.

Several high-profile invites kept the team busy, capped by a Paris-Roubaix wildcard that threw the first-year squad straight into the deep end.

The team got some wins on the board, too .

Samuel Flórez took the final stage of the Tour of the Gila in May for the team’s first win, where Modern Adventure also won the team classification. De Bod had already claimed South Africa’s national time trial title.

Oliver’s three victories, Flórez’s Gila stage, and Pickrell’s Langkawi win make five wins in its debut year in the gutters.

Oliver supplied the team’s biggest breakthrough at the Tour de Wallonie in June, winning two stages and the overall against WorldTour opposition .

In an interview with Velo , Oliver said how much the opportunity race as a pro meant to him and many of his other teammates. They were from scratching out a living to being able to focus on training and performance full-time.

“If we didn’t have credibility in the peloton, I think we definitely do now,” Oliver told Velo after those first big wins. “It was just pure emotion across the line when I realized there was no one in front of me or beside me and I hit the finish line first.”

The season’s toughest blow came on August 30, when Ezra Caudell crashed at the Philadelphia Cycling Classic .

The 19-year-old American suffered severe head and chest injuries, and friends launched a fundraising campaign to support him and his family.

There was good news this week when Caudell left the hospital to begin his rehabilitation.

Going into this week, Modern Adventure ranked 35th in the UCI standings and 14th among the 16 ProTeams, ahead of Flanders-Baloise and Novo Nordisk.

A diverse calendar of racing that spanned across the United States, Europe, and Asia will give the squad a foundation of a full season of racing to build on .

To reach the Tour de France, the team will need to take another step up next season.

Hincapie and the staff will need to recruit some key riders for the team’s second season if it wants to move up the rankings. So far, there have not been any official signings.

Factor will step up as co-title sponsor for 2027, with the promise of more financial backing, rider development, and performance support.

First, there’s one more Sunday in France.

Paris-Tours is near-monument status, with 216.2km from Chartres to Tours across the rough vineyard roads. The scenery is lovely, the racing is brutal.

Oliver gives Modern Adventure a chance to squeeze result out one more result before everyone finally puts their feet up, at least for a few weeks.

Paul Seixas wins Il Lombardia (Photo: Dario Belingheri/Getty Images) (Photo: @DarioBelingheri/@GettyImages)

Paul Seixas further underlined his staggering talent with an assured win at Il Lombardia , taking the first Monument win of his career and becoming the youngest-ever winner.

The 20 year old drove forward with 19.2km to go to drop most of the other big contenders on the Civiglio, the penultimate climb of the day. He went over the top well clear of European championships runner-up Giulio Ciccone (Lidl-Trek) and Tom Pidcock (Pinarello Q36.5 Pro Cycling), with the latter being replaced by Vuelta winner Enric Mas (Movistar)

Seixas powered up the second and final ascent of the San Fermo Della Battaglia, with Mas dropping Ciccone in a bid to close up to him.

However he was far too strong, racing in well clear and savoring the biggest win of his career.

Mas raced in for second place, 48 seconds back, with Ciccone taking third in his final race for his team.

Seixas looked stunned by what he had done, and said that things hadn’t really sunk in by the time he did the post-race interview.

“It is crazy. I think I don’t realize [it] for now,” he said. “Everything went perfect, the team did a great, awesome job. Everyone pushed more than what they had to do.”

His Decathlon CMA CGM team did indeed dedicate themselves to him, helping him to save energy until it most counted.

“I had amazing legs. I had the feeling that today was a great day,” he continued. “I managed to make the difference at the moment I choose. Maybe a bit earlier because I felt like the rhythm was not high enough at the start of the climb, for me at least, to make the difference.

“So I had to accelerate early, maybe a bit too early. There were some not really steep parts, so I had to manage really well my effort and accelerate in the hard parts. I did the best TT I could, me against myself. It was crazy.”

New European champion Remco Evenepoel had to be satisfied with fourth place, something well below his pre-race ambitions. He crashed in Il Lombardia in his 2020 debut, going over the side of a bridge and falling several meters to the ground.

He fractured his pelvis and has tried to win the race several time since. He was second to Tadej Pogačar in 2024 and 2025 and with Pogačar absent due to injury, he felt he might have his big victory this time around.

That optimism was furthered by his victory in the Euros last weekend but, once the pressure was applied, he found himself slipping backwards and losing contact with the other big challengers.

Just as was the case at the worlds, he dangled off the back of the groups his rival were in, but eventually fought his way forward again towards the end. He led the sprint in for fourth place, 1:20 back, with new world champion Brandon McNulty (UAE Emirates-XRG) continuing his stomping end of season with fifth place.

“I think I had bad position going into the penultimate climb,” he said. “I made a bit of an effort to come to the front and went a little deep on the wheel of Paul and paid for it.

“I felt really good today. But then that climb, I went into the red. That was it.”

The final Monument of the season was, as ever, a very tough one. It packed in 4662 vertical meters over 239km, and was enlivened by a big breakaway sparked off 211 kilometers out by Uno-X Mobility rider Johannes Kulse.

Andrea Mifsud (Team Polti VisitMalta), Micahel Leonard, Ben O’Connor (Jayco-AlUla) and Maxime Decomble (Groupama-FDJ United) got across, while Antonio Tiberi (Bahrain Victorious), Sylvain Moniquet (Cofidis), Fausto Masnada (MBH Bank Csb Telecom Fort), George Bennett, Pau Martí (NSN), Gijs Leemreize (Picnic PostNL) and Louis Vervaeke (Soudal Quick-Step) did likewise soon afterwards.

Julien Bernard (Lidl-Trek) and Victor Campenaerts (Visma-Lease a Bike) made it 14 and together they build a lead of almost three minutes.

O’Connor hacked down the break’s size when he set a furious pace on the Ghisallo. Their lead was 1:29 with 61.5km remaining, with the pace heating up behind when Louis Barre (Visma-Lease a Bike) went all out to platform a huge move by Matteo Jorgenson.

The American was joined by compatriots Quinn Simmons (Lidl-Trek) and Brandon McNulty (UAE Emirates-XRG), as well as the Italian Christian Scaroni (XDS Astana).

However Giulio Pellizzari put in a huge effort and brought them back several kilometers later, then continued to plough along at the front for Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe. Simmons had been the fastest up the Ghisallo but had the misfortune to experience a mechanical, ruining his chances.

Pellizzari continued to set a determined pace on the climb of San Fermo Della Battaglia and put Jorgenson, Primož Roglič (Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe), Juan Ayuso (Lidl-Trek) and Lenny Martinez (Bahrain-Victorious) out the back. His efforts ensured the break had just 44 seconds crossing the finish line with 21.8km to go, and while Leonard pushed clear alone soon afterwards on the climb of Civiglio, he was reeled in soon afterwards.

Isaac Del Toro was the big hope for UAE and Adam Yates did most of the work on that climb. However it was Seixas who was strongest. He stomped away with 19.2km remaining, Pidcock and Ciccone clinging on briefly before being forced to slow.

Pidcock’s place in the chase was taken by soon afterwards by Mas, with the Vuelta winner dropping Ciccone on the San Fermo Della Battaglia but having zero success in trying to get back up to Seixas.

The Frenchman was absolutely flying. He may have been the youngest rider in the whole race but he was far above the level of the rest.

“It is a dream. Today my legs made me dream today and then I had an opportunity,” he smiled.

“I really trained hard for this. It is incredible.”

It is, and it set things up for some fascinating clashes with Pogačar next season.

Tom Pidcock (Pinarello Q36.5 Procycling) was sixth, with nine riders in total in this group.

Thomas Silva, inset, was not seriously injured in the crash at Gran Piemonte. (Photo: Getty Images/Instagram)

Thomas Silva crashed at the final corner of Gran Piemonte on Thursday and four riders rode over him in the latest harrowing scene from a bruising week of racing in Italy .

Roadside footage captured by a fan shows the XDS-Astana rider screaming in pain as the peloton speeds past and a few even ride over his legs.

Silva was charging toward the line before he overcooked a right-hander and slammed into the fencing.

He slipped onto the asphalt and his legs were splayed into the pathway of the oncoming bunch. At least four riders struck his legs before Silva curled into the fetal position.

It’s a brutal sequence to watch. Fans frantically wave at approaching riders to slow down and steer clear, but Silva was directly in their path and there was nowhere to go for some of the ongoing riders.

Incredibly, Silva managed to stand up, get back on the bike, and finish 90th.

Team officials confirmed to Velo on Friday that the Uruguayan escaped serious injury in what was his final race of 2026.

“We had the mind and situation to end the season differently. We had a very nice season,” Silva wrote on social media. “But no complaints, thanks for the trust team!”

XDS-Astana’s Alberto Bettiol pushed on to take third behind winner Dorian Godon (Netcompany-Ineos) and Anthon Charmig (Uno-X).

Everything was coming together for Silva until the final corner.

“We were in the perfect position. Unfortunately, Thomas crashed on the final corner and wasn’t there in the final sprint,” Bettiol said. “Otherwise, I really believe we could have finished first and second. But in the end, I took third place and I’m happy with the result in the end of the season.”

For Silva, 24, it was a painful way to end a breakout season.

He won a Giro d’Italia stage and wore the maglia rosa , won back-to-back one-day wins in Spain, and a stage plus the overall at the Arctic Race of Norway.

Silva recently extended his contract through 2029, and Thursday was his last scheduled race of 2026.

Silva’s crash was the latest in a disturbing string of viral clips in a week of high-profile incidents and safety miscues across Italy.

At Monday’s Coppa Bernocchi , a DHL delivery van pulled onto the route after the breakaway passed with about 19km remaining.

Nobody crashed in that incident, and organizers later apologized.

A separate high-speed crash near the finish left Andrea Raccagni (Soudal Quick-Step) with a fractured neck vertebra. Cofidis rider Alex Aranburu fractured his collarbone and part of his pelvis.

At Tuesday’s Tre Valli Varesine, Marcel Camprubí and Thomas Gloag were involved in a collision with a police motorcycle traveling against the direction of the race .

Camprubí continued, but Gloag abandoned and needed stitches in his knee. Their Pinarello-Q36.5 captain Tom Pidcock said he was so angry he considered stopping before continuing to finish second.

“We were going 70kph on a descent and went into a round-about. We saw a motorbike coming towards us, and Thomas Gloag and me, we hit the bike,” Camprubí told Eurosport . “We are both really lucky that we were not in the hospital.

“It’s a bit frustrating, because these things happen and happen and happen, and nothing changes,” he said. “We are waiting for the facts. The team is speaking with the organization and the police, and we are still waiting for the responses.

“I think everybody can make mistakes, but when we are talking about life, we should be a bit more cautious.”

All eyes will be on Il Lombardia on Saturday, the season’s final monument and the last major race for some of the biggest stars in the elite men’s peloton.

Tadej Pogačar made “booty bands” everybody’s favorite warm-up ritual when he was filmed twerking and squatting his way through a pre-race routine, bands around his knees.

But it turns out that these wildly popular pre-ride workouts might largely be a placebo .

Waddling, lunging, and squatting through a mini-band session before a ride doesn’t “activate your glutes” or prime you to push max power.

According to WorldTour experts, the power of glute bands might largely be in the mind.

“These mini band moves are beneficial, but it’s more from a pseudo-science perspective. Someone riders might feel like, ‘Oh, I’m doing something , I’m preparing myself to ride’ by doing them,” Jayco-AlUla physiotherapist Dan Guillemette told Velo .

“But in terms of actual performance, it’s really unlikely there’s any actual benefit.”

So how have mini-bands become one of sport’s most popular primers?

They’ve become no-brainers for WorldTour and triathlon pros, TikTok influencers, 4w/kg Velo writers [ ahem ], and everyone in between.

Here’s why mini band warm-ups might not be worth your time – unless you’re already doing them – and how to make better use of these wildly popular home workout tools.

Pogačar’s pre-race warm-up video was one of the viral cycling clips of 2025. The meme pages loved it.

The Instagram reel shows Pogačar and his teammate Juan Molano working through a series of mini band exercises ahead of a stage at the UAE Tour. Pogi’s now-famous “bum to the sky” hip opener was a particular highlight.

It was a rare behind-the-scenes glimpse at how pros prepare to push wild watts for hours on end.

Since then, clips of Matteo Jorgenson , Jonas Abrahamsen , and Remco Evenepoel doing similar routines have reinforced the thinking that a few minutes inside a mini band will push you to new performance peaks.

And unlike a set of Pogačar-approved 165mm cranks or an indoor trainer “heat suit,” there’s no expensive equipment, excess sweat, or annoying apps involved.

All you need is a $10 band from Walmart and one of the routines being pumped into your cycling social feed.

The big selling point of booty band routines for cyclists and endurance athletes?

That they waken your glutes from their slumber after too long being sat on. A few minutes pushing at a mini band will buzz your butt into “workout mode.”

Strength expert Chris Peden burst that bubble when he spoke to Velo .

Peden, the head of S&C at Decathlon CMA-CGM, said pros and amateurs alike have been fooled by a misapplication of the term “sleepy glutes.”

“These routines are always advertised as ‘you’ve got weak glutes, your glutes don’t work, or are ‘asleep.’ That’s the result of medical terms transferring to the performance world that don’t really apply,” Peden told Velo . “It’s a medical term from those who are extremely inactive, not somebody who does even a low level of training.

“And anyway, muscles don’t ‘switch on’ or ‘switch off,’” Peden continued. “Your neuromuscular system is always working. Your brain knows exactly what to recruit at any one time,” Peden said.

“A band workout does not make that signal ‘better’ or ‘cleaner,’ as some suggest. It’s unlikely to have any benefit at all.”

If you’re reading this post, you’re likely interested in bikes and maybe ride one every so often.

A second misconception? That squeezing some torque out of your glutes with an oversized elastic band will ready you for your 400-watt interval workout.

That’s founded in another misapplication, this time of the term “PAP.”

PAP, or Post Activation Potentiation, refers to the acute boost in muscular performance following a previous activity. A set of heavy back squats before attempting a maximum vertical jump is a common real-world application of PAP.

But sadly, a set of waddling “monster walks” won’t come close to delivering the muscular force or speed required for any meaningful PAP.

In the world’s biggest bike races, turbo trainers – not mini bands – are used to provide an effective potentiation.

These torture devices are wheeled out of team trucks ahead of time trials, hard uphill starts, or for those wanting to make the day’s early break. Riders work through a progressive build before a series of short submaximal efforts that fully stimulate the muscles for a fast racing start.

So, wait one sec. If the popular theories behind booty bands are a load of BS, why are they still so popular in the dialed-down, scientifically-backed WorldTour?

Even Peden admitted his own athletes on Decathlon CMA-CGM do them, even though he dismisses their direct impact on performance. Both he and Guillemette at Jayco-AlUla think that for many riders, the gains are all in the mind.

For many, workout bands became part of their pre-ride routine as juniors, either as a misguided warm-up tool or as a minimal dose of strength work.

“Psychologically, the placebo effect is massive,” Peden said. “Our riders still do them regardless of what we might say. They’ve been told to do it since they were 15 years old, and that it’s beneficial to them. So I can’t turn around to tell them to suddenly stop.

“They’re not doing any harm, but they’re not achieving anything meaningful as a supposed ‘activation,’” he continued. “If they’re proving some psychological benefit and riders believe they help, I’m not going to hold them back. However, I might try to suggest they include some more useful practices, instead – say, around mobility.”

Guillemette, who worked at Team Sky before he joined Jayco-AlUla, added that a band routine can also help riders transition out of inactivity.

They prime the mind and loosen the body.

“It’s really unlikely that there’s any benefit to using bands in terms of race performance,” Guillemette said.…

Pierina Nicuray, a 21-year-old university graduate, has spent a week camped out in Madrid's Puerta del Sol square.

Like many of the hundreds of others who have pitched their tents here to protest at Spain's housing crisis , she has no doubts when it comes to diagnosing the cause.

"It's the same problem as always," she says. "A lack of homes."

She adds: "Landlords are taking advantage of the situation to raise rentals, and then there's also Airbnb."

Jorge Moreno, a 19-year-old film-dubbing student who has also been living in a tent here in central Madrid for the last few days, agrees.

"There are so many homes standing empty because they have been bought by vulture funds and investment funds which hike up the rent of people living in properties until they get rid of them," says Jorge, who lives with his mother and fears it will be a long time before he can afford a home of his own.

"They've been making a business of housing for a long time," he adds. "But it's an abusive business which stops Spaniards from being able to live in a decent home."

His and Pierina's diagnoses are frequently voiced by fellow protesters, ordinary Spaniards and even the Spanish government.

On presenting a recent package of emergency measures to tackle the housing problem, Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said he was legislating "against those who consider housing just another object on the market with which to speculate".

Those reforms were rejected by Congress, prompting Sánchez to call a snap election next month.

Nicuray and Moreno can point to the single case that sparked the current Spanish housing protest movement as proof that profit-driven practices are at the heart of the crisis: the 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal was evicted from her home after the investment firm that had bought it tried to persuade her to leave, then sharply increased her rent, which she was unable to pay.

Although the social backlash that followed caused the company to invite Abascal to return to her old home, she never did, dying in hospital on Wednesday .

Many others have their own stories of struggling with a soaring rental market.

Carmen Pérez is a retired widow, originally from Ecuador, who has been living in Spain for 17 years.

When she arrived, housing was relatively cheap and accessible, but - as costs have risen - she has been forced to move in with her daughter and son-in-law as she looks for somewhere affordable to rent.

"When a property is listed to rent, there's always a long waiting list," she says. "And the rent is always too high for me. All of this has affected my health - I've got depression, I don't have any stability or security."

Spain has seen an average rise in rental costs of 84% over the last 10 years, according to property outlet Idealista.

In the centre of the southern city of Málaga, the increase has been 113 %, and, in Marbella - just under 150%.

Such numbers have made housing Spaniards' biggest concern.

A recent study by the Centre for Sociological Research (CIS) showed how the broader Spanish population, like the protesters, want to see action taken against those perceived to be powerful movers in the housing market.

Some 72% wanted higher taxes introduced for those with 10 or more properties; 76% wanted limits on short-term tourist accommodation; and 40% supported the expropriation of empty homes.

However, Jorge Galindo, director at the Esade centre for economic policy, says that available data makes it difficult to know exactly how many Spanish properties are owned by so-called "vulture funds" and being used for speculation.

He points to Bank of Spain figures from 2024 showing that only 8% of properties for rent are owned by companies.

Galindo says he concludes from the data available that there is not a notable accumulation of property to rent among a small number of owners in Spain.

"When it comes to explaining the rise in rentals, that is not the big cause," he says. "What explains it is the shortage of supply compared to demand over recent years."

The Bank of Spain appears to agree, and has estimated that the country has a housing shortfall of around 750,000 homes.

The institution's deputy governor, Soledad Núñez, warned in September that by 2028 that could rise to one million.

There are 3.8 million empty properties in Spain, according to the National Statistics Institute (INE), but a large number of those are in depopulated rural areas and therefore have little relevance to the current crisis, which is most acute in urban hubs.

Other explanations for this high number include properties awaiting renovation, or legal disputes between family members who have inherited them.

Demographic changes play a major part in the imbalance between supply and demand.

Between 2021 and 2025, there were about 1.2 million new households in Spain, driven in great part by the arrival of migrants who have played a major role in the country's recent economic growth.

However, house building has not kept pace, with fewer than half-a-million new homes during that period.

That was partly because Spain's construction industry had shrunk in the wake of the Eurozone crisis, while the cost of materials rose substantially after Covid, and a lack of political consensus put legal obstacles in the way of building.

"It was not a priority for us to build new houses," Galindo says. "But, once the demographic boom came, we realised how costly it was for us."

He adds that short-term tourist accommodation, like Airbnb, which has been identified by both the Spanish government and many activists as a culprit, is likely to have had a more localised effect, pushing up prices in specific urban areas rather than having an overall impact.

Meanwhile, the crisis has been aggravated by lagging salaries.…

Asos has told its customers hackers are in possession of detailed profiles of potentially millions of the online store's users.

It issued the update after BBC News told the retailer it had been contacted by cyber criminals who said this week's breach went beyond "basic contact details" Asos previously said might have been accessed.

Names, addresses, phone numbers, emails and customer numbers are now in the hands of cyber criminals.

So too are the searches customers have made on the website. Terms like "reclaimed vintage", "glamorous wide fit" and "Asos petite" are visible in the data.

With this information, scammers may be able to craft potent phishing attack emails or phone calls.

The risk to individuals is now higher and customers are being warned about potential impersonation scams.

In its email to customers, Asos confirmed data profiles were taken but said no bank details or passwords were accessed.

"Please remain cautious of unexpected messages or calls claiming to be from Asos," it said.

"We will never ask you to share passwords, security codes or payment details through an unsolicited message or call."

The company did not respond to questions about the scale of the breach.

The high profile hack made global headlines on Tuesday when cyber criminals used Asos's own app system to send a pop up notification to potentially millions of people.

Later that day the firm confirmed to shareholders via the London Stock Exchange that the pop up was sent by an "unauthorised third party" and "basic personal information including name and contact details may have been accessed."

The company then sent an email to customers with similar wording.

On Wednesday evening the cyber criminals responsible contacted the BBC sharing a sample of the stolen data which showed the true extent of the hack.

The BBC held off publishing this article to allow Asos to contact its customers first.

Asos said it is still investigating how the hack happened.

It told customers hackers "gained access to an Asos employee account by impersonating a trusted contact to obtain log in credentials".

With that log in to an unnamed service, the hackers were able to download the customer data.

In the pop up notification send to customers by the hackers, they claimed they had "compromised the Snowflake instance".

Snowflake is a popular data storage and analysis company whose customers have been breached in the past due to unauthorised log ins.

The cyber criminals, calling themselves Xuanyewen, claimed to the BBC they used a platform which is built natively on top of Snowflake - called Simon AI - to gain access to the data.

Simon AI has been contacted for comment. Snowflake previously said its platform had not been breached.

Asos said customers are not being asked to take any action.

But cyber security experts have warned users to change passwords as a precaution and be on alert for suspicious activity.

Asos said its website and app are safe to use and "we know our customers trust us with their information".

"We take that responsibility seriously and have already taken additional steps to further strengthen security controls," it said.

Donald Trump's decision to import Russian fuel to the US represents a remarkable about-face from the president.

Just three weeks ago, Trump signed legislation to authorise fresh American sanctions and tariffs on nations that import Russian oil and gas.

Now, Trump says, Russian President Vladimir Putin has agreed to supply hundreds of thousands of tons of diesel fuel to the US and world markets in the coming months.

The deal comes as Trump is still grappling with the political fallout of the Iran war and its impact on global energy prices, weeks before American voters head to the polls in the midterm elections.

As the cost of fuel has skyrocketed in America, his standing with the public – stung by the higher prices at the pump and knock-on effects that led to across-the board inflation – has soured.

The toll the war is taking has been acutely felt by US agricultural states, which rely heavily on diesel to operate farming machinery and to transport their products to market.

It is these states – places like Iowa, Kansas, Texas and Ohio – that have become unexpected political battlegrounds in the upcoming elections that will determine if Republicans maintain control of Congress.

Trump announces deal for Russian diesel as Zelensky criticises 'gift to Putin'

What are the US midterms? A simple guide

For months, the American president has been searching for ways to ease his party's political pain.

He recently pressured European allies to further tap their oil reserves . He deferred federal taxes on the fuel and authorised supplies designated for farm use to be used in interstate trucking.

He has also promised that he would not renew attacks on Iran until after the midterms – an unusually frank acknowledgement of the political impact the ongoing conflict is having.

His decision to strike a deal with Russia's Putin is only the latest, most dramatic effort.

Trump's Truth Social posts often provide incomplete information, of course. The details of exactly how Russia is supplying this fuel to the global market, and what they might get for in return – besides much-needed hard currency – is unclear.

It opens Trump to criticism from European allies and American politicians that his administration is now helping to fund the Russian war machine.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky called the deal a "gift" to Putin that Russia would "repay" with "terror and perfidy".

"Allowing Russia to sell petroleum products is an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged," he wrote on X.

It is also uncertain exactly how much Trump's move will help Republicans at the ballot box.

The promised European diesel release hasn't moved energy prices significantly, and there's no information on the speed with which Russian fuel could enter the market.

Its diesel refinery capacity has been damaged by repeated Ukrainian strikes – attacks that Trump has encouraged Zelensky to curtail.

The US uses approximately 3.6 million barrels of diesel a day, so even if Russia delivers its promised 300,000 tons this month, that amounts to approximately half of the US daily consumption.

Americans may not notice much of an immediate difference.

With less than a month before November's midterm elections, early voting has already started in many states. The political cake, as the saying goes, is all but baked.

"Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my Greatest Priority," Trump wrote in his Truth Social post.

But over the past seven months, prices on energy, fuel and consumer goods have only gone up - even as Trump and his officials have repeatedly assured an uneasy public a successful resolution to the war, and an easing of its economic impact, is nearly at hand.

Trump may be left hoping that his latest deal, setting aside its potentially uncomfortable diplomatic issues, will be enough to convince American voters that his promise of impending economic relief is more than just empty words.

Trump wants to reduce the cost of fuel as the midterms loom - will it work?

If you have been looking to buy a health or beauty product, the chances are you will have shopped at a Boots somewhere in the UK.

The pharmacy and retailer is a stalwart of Britain's high streets, where it has served generations of customers for decades.

But now it is set to enter its 178th year under new ownership after an £7bn deal was agreed this week - here's three ways it could affect your shopping experience.

Upgrading its portfolio of 1,800 stores is high on the list of Boots' new owners, Wittington Investments. This is the holding company of the Westons - a wealthy and retail-steeped Canadian family who used to own Selfridges and currently own several large retailers across the Atlantic.

The UK branch of the family also controls the owner of Primark, Associated British Foods (ABF).

What Boots stores might look like in the future has not been disclosed.

Business has been good for Boots in recent years, and new-look beauty areas in some of its bigger shops have given shoppers more of a department store experience, according to Sofie Willmott, an associate director and analyst at GlobalData Retail.

Since the opening of its first beauty-only store in 2023 in the Battersea Power Station development, it says it has redesigned over 180 beauty halls, while also opening its first fragrance concept store and an Opticians dedicated to luxury eyewear.

"They should invest in the rest of the chain because they've got such a big store portfolio that I think some of the smaller stores have really lacked investment over time, and I think that is something that they need to kind of catch up with," Willmott says.

A more "consistent" look would also be an improvement, Willmott adds. "At the moment there is a bit of a disconnect."

Jackie Naghten, a retail industry veteran who has worked for the likes of Top Shop, Marks & Spencer and Debenhams, thinks Boots' stores need to be made "more functional" by not having their health hubs "squeezed in the corner".

But Yasmin Trimble, 22, who buys beauty products from Boots, likes how the easy stores are to navigate.

"You can get everything you need...it is not confusing. It has got a cleaner aesthetic to it as well."

Boots was an early adopter of the loyalty cards commonly offered today by companies offering points and discounts to customers who sign up.

Its Advantage card, launched in 1997, is unlikely to go away and remains popular.

Naghten doesn't think they would get rid of it. "It's the best-value store card in terms of bang for your buck."

The card offers shoppers three points for every pound they spend. Each point is worth 1p.

Katie Burrows, 23, is a fan of building up the points to get money off.

She mainly shops at Boots for skincare, first aid and medicine, but thinks prices for its sanitary products are "ridiculously expensive" - something her friend Yasmin agrees with.

Lewis Harrison believes the loyalty card is also good value, but finds it "frustrating how the rewards points only cover a full transaction".

"I wish you could use your points for a partial transaction like you can in Holland and Barrett," the 25-year-old says. "It would be good to use the points towards more expensive transactions."

Natalie Berg, retail expert and founder of consultancy NBK Retail, suggests the Advantage card gives Boots "a unique understanding of their customers" and is an asset the new owners "will want to double down on".

"As AI and social media change how people discover and buy products, that direct relationship with customers will only become more important."

The new owners have already signalled they plan to expand Boots' healthcare service, a booming industry at the moment.

The retailer started out as an apothecary, so health is in its roots. Today, it offers a wide range of health and wellbeing services as well as prescriptions and vaccinations through its in-store pharmacies.

It also announced earlier this summer it was expanding services for weight loss drugs, which have surged in popularity.

Naghten points out that the Weston family's purchase of Boots comes at a time when pharmacies are increasingly going to prescribe more medications and health services, in a bid to ease pressure on GP surgeries and hospitals.

"They didn't buy this thing for no reason. They have got the blueprint," she says.

While health will remain a core part of its business, Boots has other strengths, Naghten adds, in its No7 make-up and skincare products.

"When you have all these people coming in for health and wellbeing services, they will also be picking up a lipstick," she says.

Willmott suggests Boots has an "edge" over its rivals on the health side, given its reputation as an expert.

But the company is facing tough competition, which Boots acknowledged affected revenues in its latest financial results.

Shoppers, particularly younger ones, are increasingly seeking products online through influencer ads rather than heading to brick-and-mortar shops.

There are also other big players, such as Superdrug. And M&S this week announced a new partnership with Sephora, saying it would replace a hundred of its own beauty departments with the brand next year.

For 18-year-old Schekina Bourne, Boots is not a "go-to shop" for her. "Even though I can go to Boots even in my area....Superdrug is like closest to me. So, I'll prefer the convenience," she says.

Additional reporting by Ben Sturt and Anuk Weerawardana

Andy Burnham has promised to curb companies' ability to restrict what their workers can do after leaving their job.

In a speech, the prime minister said the use of non-compete clauses in employment contracts had "gone too far" and was holding innovative UK companies back.

He added the clauses had forced workers to go without pay after leaving a role, as well as making it harder for growing firms to hire new staff.

Ahead of the Budget later this month, he also said there was "more to do" on tax to encourage promising firms to stay in the UK.

Sir Keir Starmer's government had been exploring possible restrictions on non-compete clauses since late last year, including a total ban, banning them above a certain salary threshold, or limiting how long they can last.

Although commonly associated with the financial services and technology sectors, research cited by the government has estimated around 5 million jobs in Britain are covered by the clauses, typically lasting around six months.

Speaking at a business summit in Manchester, Burnham confirmed his government would press ahead with new legislation to ensure the clauses can "no longer be a barrier" to hiring new staff.

He added that their use had stopped workers leaving to join other companies, or founding their own firms instead, adding: "I think that's a drag on innovation."

Referencing a landmark 1995 court ruling that is credited with revolutionising the football transfer market in Europe, he said he hoped reining in non-compete clauses could prove the "Bosman ruling for the innovation sector".

Burnham did not specify the scope of the restrictions he is planning, but suggested they would apply to the "everyday economy" as well as helping "promising start-ups and scaling firms".

It is understood that the government is planning to unveil details of the proposed restrictions, which were first reported by Politico , external and The Financial Times , external , alongside the Budget on 28 October.

Responding to the prime minister's comments, the Recruitment and Employment Confederation warned against "sweeping" changes to non-compete rules, adding they played a "vital role" in protecting commercially sensitive information and client relationships.

The previous Conservative government had ruled out a total ban , external on non-compete clauses, after hearing from employers that it could reduce investor confidence in the UK or prompt companies to tighten how they share information internally.

The prime minister sought to frame the announcement on non-compete clauses as part of a wider government pitch to boost innovative sectors of the economy.

He told the summit that although the UK was home to outstanding research and start-ups, too many companies had gone abroad in search of investment.

He also signalled that the government would "say more" at the Budget about plans to use public investment as a way to encourage private funding in the economy.

He added that he wanted all UK regions to have a dedicated fund to do this, modelled on the Good Growth Fund launched in Greater Manchester last year, during his tenure as mayor of the city-region.

He also hinted that the government was looking at the tax system to ensure the UK can retain high-growth companies.

He said: "One of our biggest challenges is breaking through our own ceiling. Too often, our best ideas are developed and scaled overseas, and with it the jobs, technology and investment that goes with them."

"So I know there is more to do to fix that, specifically on tax, to encourage people to stay and scale."

On 23 August, Cooper Freeman had no idea clouds above his head were being filled with a silver compound in order to cause rainfall.

Neither did thousands of other residents in Homer, Alaska, who later discovered San Francisco start-up Rainmaker conducted an experiment in that region using cloud-seeding technology.

The company claims it produced 19 million US gallons of water in the sky in three hours.

This approach to weather modification, now more than 80-years-old, involves using planes and drones to disperse compounds such as silver iodide into clouds to form ice crystals. Those crystals eventually become large enough to fall as rain or snow, depending on the temperatures below.

Essentially, cloud seeding speeds up the natural process of water vapor condensing inside of clouds. Gravity then pulls those crystals to the ground. The technology, though, needs ideal climate environments, such as mountainous or cold regions such as Alaska.

Freeman, the Alaska director of the Center for Biological Diversity, isn't just concerned Homer residents weren't widely alerted to these experiments. He's sceptical about what was shot into the clouds, and questions how safe it was for both residents and their habitat.

"It doesn't appear that there was any downstream monitoring to verify that this silver iodide didn't impact the environment," he says.

Freeman adds, "Having a company come in to do this seeding isn't going to solve our water woes, and it feels like a distraction from solving the urgent issues related to water conservation."

Concerns are mounting about the challenges surrounding water security. United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres said in July "our world is using freshwater faster than it can be replenished , external ", which echoes reports noting how the past five years have led to the driest period for global rivers , external in more than three decades.

Cloud-seeding technology may be a drop in the bucket, as it doesn't create rainstorms. For example, Rainmaker's 19 million gallons equates to around 0.01 inch of rain across 100 square miles.

Nevertheless, more than 50 countries , external are developing programmes to modify the weather and a surge of start-ups are developing systems to create rain.

As well developed and promising as this innovative field has become, these businesses continue to face thorny questions on safety and efficacy, leading to novel approaches with both finding the right material to spray into clouds and how they do it.

Augustus Doricko, the founder and CEO of Rainmaker, is quick to answer any questions on the consequences of how his company uses the silver iodide compound. It's clear he's been asked about chemical safety many times.

He says Rainmaker releases this form of silver at 20 grams per flight, distributed across thousands of square kilometres. "The resultant increase in concentration on the ground is in the parts per quadrillion, way below the threshold laid out by the FDA [Food and Drug Administration] on what is allowable."

Rainmaker's flights use drones to soar into clouds because without clouds, "we can't do anything," he says, pointing to one of the key limits of cloud-seeding processes. Cloud-seeding sessions have to wait for clouds to form to try to coax them into precipitation.

Their drones are outfitted with silver iodide flairs, and when lit the burning atomizes the water particles into a small enough size so they can stay suspended in the freezing cloud for hours, eventually turning into crystals and later rain.

Rainmaker operates in states such as Idaho, Utah, Colorado and areas of the Middle East such as Jordan. Doricko says, "Jordan residents often only have water for hours per week from their utility because of how scarce water is, and it's a privilege to try to help this storied region."

Cloud seeding's roots began in 1946 when researchers from the General Electric Research Laboratory used dry ice as the first seeding agent. A year later, silver iodide was found to be more effective than dry ice, which quickly turns into useless gas.

While seeding agents caused more rainfall, they didn't move the needle much. In fact, sobering statistics point to how patchy this technology can be in what it pours on the ground.

"With the right conditions, cloud seeding squeeze out about an extra five to 10% of precipitation," says Jon Meyer, an assistant state climatologist with the Utah Climate Center.

What was encouraging, though, for the cloud-seeding sector was a landmark 2017 study that found how silver iodide worked as expected, one of the first reports to observe cloud seeding in action using radar and precipitation gauges.

In the past several years, Meyer has been encouraged to see more companies such as Rainmaker bring innovation to an old industry. "Drones [such as Rainmaker's products] present this new avenue," says Meyer, "and they offer a more targeted nature to these clouds we hope will be responsive."

What is sprayed into clouds may also be undergoing a major shift. Recast Systems in San Francisco is experimenting with a type of protein made from amino acids found in the soil, says CEO Olivia Li.

While still undergoing tests at Texas A&M University, this new seeding agent moves Recast away from silver iodide as the go-to compound.

"It's safe, biodegradable and nucleates ice at a higher efficiency than silver iodide," says Li, whose company currently uses silver iodide to seed clouds in several US states.

Meyer is optimistic this technology's trajectory will only continue to rise. "We're going to see more demand for these services as so many regions are experiencing water demand," he says, "and they're going to be looking for ways to help bridge that gap."

A Londonderry company has become one of the UK's biggest car park operators after buying NCP out of administration.

The deal means the Martin Group will control more than 100 sites.

The NCP business collapsed in March 2026 after a sustained period of declining performance left it unable to pay its debts.

At that time some of its sites were closed or transferred to other operators.

The administrators, PwC, said the majority of NCP's 145 sites would now transfer to the Martin Group along with the staff who work there.

Zelf Hussain, joint administrator and partner at PwC, said the deal protected hundreds of jobs and delivered the best outcome for creditors.

"Keeping NCP's car parks open also helps keep Britain's town and city centres moving," he added.

"We would like to thank all of NCP's staff and directors for their support and professionalism throughout what has understandably been a period of uncertainty."

NCP's major problems included being locked into long-term leases with property owners and building up a large amount of debt.

The Martin Group already has a substantial commercial property portfolio across the UK including the Fishergate Shopping Centre in Preston and the Mercury Shopping Centre in Romford.

It has recently expanded its hotels business, developing The Bedford Hotel in Belfast and buying The Waterfoot in Derry.

Gary Martin, director of Martin Property Group, said the company's goal was to "build on the strength and heritage of the NCP brand so it can once again deliver the lasting impact on the communities it serves".

"NCP is an iconic brand with a loyal customer base and talented workforce," he added.

Rob England, chief executive of NCP, said it was "a fantastic day for NCP".

"We have had to make difficult, necessary decisions to keep the business moving forward," he said.

England said NCP was "immensely grateful" to its employees, customers and suppliers and its priority was "to restore full operational momentum and build a sustainable platform for long-term growth".

The Claude-maker said on Thursday it was updating its usage policy to let its tools end interactions where people are "cruel" - something it said it had done in "rare" cases prior.

It will now be included on a list of forbidden conduct which also contains bullying others, promoting self-harm and creating non-consensual intimate imagery.

While Anthropic said the policy would only apply in "extreme cases" of repeated abuse, it has reignited debate over how we should communicate with AI tools.

The company said it would not apply to "common versions of user frustration, pushback, dark creative themes, or model testing and research" - suggesting it would only apply in clearly deliberate instances.

But what Anthropic would consider "abusive or cruel behaviour" towards its models remains unclear.

Screenshots of the new policy have been widely shared and commented on across social media - with some praising it as advancing good manners or "model welfare".

But others criticised the plan, with one person calling it " deeply wrong , external " and another suggesting it might undermine abuse directed at humans and animals.

"You can't be cruel to numbers and maths," wrote Dr Barry Scannell, technology partner at Irish law firm William Fry, on LinkedIn , external .

"This level of anthropomorphisation of AI is harmful. It leads people to believe that it's something it's not."

Microsoft AI director Mustafa Suleyman, who in September criticised rival firm Anthropic for treating AI like it is human , reacted to Anthropic's update with a melting face emoji.

What is AI, how does it work and why are some people concerned about it?

The people who think AI might become conscious

The changes, first reported by tech outlet The Verge, came following an annual review of the usage policy at the firm.

It was also updated to address new or emerging risks in other areas, including by forbidding use of Claude for "deceptive campaigns" or clarifying that, as US midterm elections loom , it cannot be used to "deceive voters or disrupt elections".

Anthropic also said on Thursday its usage policy previously prevented its tools being used to develop weapons.

But none of the updates have attracted as much attention or scrutiny as its move to forbid users abusing its chatbots.

It has also tapped into the much-debated question of whether we should be curt or polite when using generative AI tools.

Some experts say writing or saying "please" or "thank you" to tools like ChatGPT is unnecessary and wastes tokens - used by the large language models powering generative AI tools to process and reply to you.

Others argue politeness can lead to higher quality answers or responses.

When a X user last year asked about electricity costs incurred by ChatGPT replying to users' "please" and "thank you" messages, OpenAI boss Sam Altman said it was , external "tens of millions of dollars well spent - you never know".

The Collins Dictionary meanwhile last November highlighted the re-emergence of the term "clanker" for disparagingly referring to AI tools .

Used to describe robots in Star Wars games and movies since the mid 2000s, the term made its shortlist of words reflecting the mood of 2025 after last July saw many take to TikTok to share their frustrations with AI-powered machines.

Some experts have also posited that being rude to AI chatbots could adversely impact human communication, by seeping into how we talk to and treat others.

Why friendly AI chatbots might be less trustworthy

Why are there concerns AI could threaten humanity, and how real are they?

More than 260 industry leaders from business, finance and law have held a meeting to discuss the role high value residents play in Jersey's economy.

Jersey's high value residency programme , external grants residential status to highly skilled and economically active high net worth individuals.

One attendee at the Chamber of Commerce lunch on Thursday, Mary O'Keeffe, said high value residents "were extremely important" to the island.

However, one former economic advisor to the government described the tax contribution of high value residents as "piffling".

About 260 families currently live in Jersey having relocated through the scheme.

O'Keeffe who runs Mary O'Keeffe relocation , external to help high value residents settle in the island said they contributed a lot to the economy and philanthropic causes.

"They are extremely important, so here today the room is full of private bankers, tax accountants, lawyers, people like myself and professionals who all work with high net individuals.

"So, they bring an enormous amount to the economy and that doesn't even touch on what they bring in regard to philanthropy."

High value residents pay a 20% tax rate on the first £1.25m of worldwide income , external .

They then pay a 1% on any income above £1.25m and there are some who feel these individuals should be paying more tax , external .

O'Keeffe said: "I can understand that but that's not looking at the argument the right way.

"First of all, the basic pay that they pay is £250,000 and that's before you even look at their worldwide income.

"And the 1% often equates to many millions and that's what people don't understand.

"High net worth individuals are extremely mobile, they are fluid, they can pick up and go wherever they want and they want to go somewhere that's safe, that's secure, that their wealth is going to be looked after and they're not going to feel that they're going to be ripped off."

Garry Bell, a tax advisor to high value residents, said if tax for wealthy individuals was increased he believed Jersey would lose them.

He said if the money they made above £1.25m was taxed at 20% instead of 1% it could damage the economy.

"If we tax those individuals at 20% the numbers would reduce dramatically. So instead of having a net increase of say 18 or19 individuals a year you're probably only looking at one or two," Bell said.

"So, we're sacrificing by seeking to tax them more, we're sacrificing that the direct income tax take, the stamp duty take, the employment, the GST, there's a whole raft of economic benefits that we sacrifice by actually seeking to tax those individuals at 20%.

"We are competing with a number of other jurisdictions, Dubai - zero tax. Monaco - zero tax.

"We're already one of the most expensive jurisdictions."

John Christensen, a former economic advisor to Jersey's government in the 1980s and 1990s was critical of the High Value Residents programme.

He said the amount of tax they pay is "piffling, frankly".

"I think it's quite divisive, particularly in such an unequal island community.

"As a development strategy, who benefits? They benefit because they're paying very little tax on their income but is it going to benefit young Jersey people? Not at all.

"I suspect its going to contribute more to ratcheting up of house prices, ratcheting up of prices in the shops, and a higher cost of living generally.

"And where they contribute to the island's economy, outside paying frankly minimal amounts of tax, lies with construction work.

"They've built endless, frankly, rather ugly and inappropriately sized houses."

It's green, bulging and intimidating. Ford's latest vehicle looks like a pick-up truck that has been through an Incredible Hulk transformation. Based on its popular Ranger series, this beefy number parked outside the front door of Ford's Dagenham plant can carry a load of two tonnes, tow up to four tonnes and is also shouldering the hopes of the 2,000-strong workforce that still makes engines here.

Inside the factory, the three-litre diesel engines that will power this camo-painted beast drift down a production line that has seen output cut from 90,000 engines a year to about half that over the last decade.

Ford is hoping that a pivot towards military vehicles can help fill the void created by what the company's UK boss calls the most challenging environment since the invention of the motor car. Once mighty, the European car industry is starting to look puny and is hoping surging defence budgets as Europe re-arms can help it flex its industrial muscles once more.

Ford is part of a joint venture with defence specialists General Dynamics and Ricardo bidding for a Ministry of Defence (MoD) contract to supply 9,000 vehicles over the next five to seven years to replace the Army's ageing Land Rover-based fleet.

Lisa Brankin, chair of Ford UK, says it is a chance to showcase their abilities to respond quickly to defence needs: "As a manufacturer you look at every opportunity that comes at you and this is a great opportunity that we would love to take advantage of."

This is not the first time Ford has busied itself with defence work.

Ahead of World War Two, Ford's factory in Dagenham, east London, was the largest car plant in Europe.

When war broke out, civilian car assembly stopped completely, and the factory was converted entirely to military production. Between 1939 and 1945, the Dagenham plant built 360,000 vehicles for the Allied war effort.

Ford workers in Manchester manufactured 34,000 Rolls-Royce-designed Merlin engines, which powered Spitfires and Hurricane fighter planes.

Eighty years later, the UK and European car industries are hoping that the engines of war can help defend against what one supplier told the BBC was a "terminal decline".

As Europe feels compelled to commit hundreds of billions to ramp up defence spending in the face of the menace from Russia and US reluctance to be Europe's protector, car makers that are under commercial attack from Chinese rivals have taken notice.

So can the rearmament of Europe save an auto industry and a supply chain facing crisis?

Ford is far from the only car company that sees defence as a growth industry - and one that can utilise the growing overcapacity at car plants across Europe.

French car maker Renault has signed a strategic agreement with defence giant Thales to produce military drones - targeting an output of up to 1,000 units per month. The French military and Directorate General for Armament want to tap into Renault's mass-production capabilities to bypass traditional, slower defence supply chains.

Meanwhile, Volkswagen has agreed to sell an under-used factory in Osnabruck, western Germany, which will become a military manufacturing hub in a joint venture with an Israeli-based defence investor.

Jaguar Land Rover (JLR), which makes the Land Rover, is also bidding for the same contract as Ford - as the Army retires its existing Land Rover-based fleet by 2030. JLR has also established a new dedicated business unit to support its global military ambitions.

It makes sense for under-utilised auto manufacturing capacity to switch to defence, says Mike Hawes of the Society for Motor Manufacturers and Traders (SMMT) trade association.

The UK car industry and its suppliers are heavily reliant on a few big manufacturers – Nissan in Sunderland, Toyota in Derbyshire, BMW in Oxfordshire and the biggest of them all by value of output, JLR at multiple sites in the Midlands and Merseyside.

And Hawes says the supply chain is very vulnerable.

"UK automotive output has been in decline over the last eight or nine years," he says. "We're probably half of what we were 10 years ago. Now, that's obviously going to hit the supply chain because they're not making the same number of parts. So they've got capacity. They may be quite dependent on one particular manufacturer as well."

So they will welcome "the opportunity to broaden their customer base and potentially move into defence", he says.

Just two weeks ago, JLR announced it was cutting 4,000 jobs from its 30,000-strong UK workforce in order to reduce costs to stay competitive with international – particularly Chinese – rivals. Dave Roberts of the firm Evtec, which supplies cooling systems components to JLR, is worried about the implications of this.

"JLR is the critical mass in the UK automotive manufacturing space," he says. "It is the glue that holds the whole of the sector together. Because remember, when you're making volumes for JLR, they're significantly higher than any other car maker in the UK.

"If they suffer, the ripples run deeper through the supply chain."

Earlier this week, major JLR suppliers urged the government to help automotive manufacturers move into aerospace and defence, warning that large-scale car production in the UK faces long-term decline.

In an open letter to the prime minister, chancellor and West Midlands Mayor Richard Parker, industry leaders argued Britain's automotive supply chain was "not in decline" but "in the wrong market".

The letter was signed by executives representing businesses with more than 8,600 direct employees, alongside the Confederation of British Metalforming, which represents about 75,000 workers.

Signatories to the letter said the redundancies were "the first visible crack" in a UK automotive supply chain supporting about 183,000 manufacturing jobs.…

Brighton & Hove Albion owner Tony Bloom says he is looking forward to seeing what the Seagulls can achieve after results he described as the "best in the history of the football club".

In a rare interview, Bloom told BBC South East victory over Manchester United in the Carabao Cup, a 3-0 win over champions Arsenal, and the 5-0 thrashing of Coventry City had boosted confidence at the club.

Bloom helped transform Brighton's fortunes after he became majority shareholder at the club in 2009, when the team were struggling in the third tier of English football and playing at a temporary ground.

"(I'm) looking forward to what this team can achieve this season", Bloom said.

The Seagulls are currently third in the Premier League and are tipped to win the Europa Conference League.

Bloom's grandfather Harry was vice-chairman at the club in the 1970s, and he's been a fan since childhood.

He would watch them play at the Goldstone Ground, which Brighton were forced to leave due to debt in 1997.

The club were promoted to the Premier League eight years after he took control and celebrated its 125 -year anniversary at the victory over Arsenal on 19 September.

That win was three days after coming back from 2-0 down to knock Manchester United out of the League Cup at Old Trafford, and they beat Coventry the weekend before.

Bloom's leadership and sustainable business model - buying and selling players at a huge profit with a data-led approach - has become the envy of clubs worldwide.

Brighton, however, have not won silverware since promotion, and Bloom doesn't dwell on their successes so far.

"It's vital that we always look forward, there's no point in looking back," he said.

"We're always looking to improve in everything we do in terms of performances, in terms of results, processes, innovative way of doing things because our competition is doing the same so if you stand still you go backwards.

"So we enjoy the moments and then move on because we have to keep improving."

Brighton are about to start their second ever European campaign, this time in the Conference League, a cup that rivals Crystal Palace won last season.

"Obviously, winning leagues, winning trophies is really difficult, but I do think we've got a real chance," Bloom said.

"The Conference League is a very winnable tournament compared to others we've played in."

Bloom said he also hoped Brighton's women's side would win a trophy this season.

Having bankrolled the building of Brighton's Amex Stadium, he said he is now "really excited" about the club's plans for a new £80m women's stadium .

He added: "Having a stadium right next to the Amex is perfect for us."

"I'm really looking forward to 2030 when hopefully the players will be walking out at our new stadium."
